domain_reasoning: Apart from talking to the customer, the time goes into entering the order in the account or billing system.
length_reasoning: A simple address change takes a few minutes; a new contract with identity checks, terms and a read-back, or a discontinuance with final-bill questions, takes longer.
review_reasoning: A quality reviewer listens to the recorded contact, partly sped up, and checks the submitted order against what was said.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong address or a wrongly processed discontinuance causes misdirected bills or service loss, usually noticed and reversed after a complaint.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's order screens, products and policies, learned over a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: Most of the time goes into opening billing and account records and checking outside data such as weather in several systems.
length_reasoning: A simple bill complaint with an obvious cause takes ten minutes; a disputed usage history needing meter data, weather and past contacts takes an hour or more.
review_reasoning: A supervisor reads the finding and checks the key records it cites; a typical case needs several records re-opened.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong finding leads to a wrong refund or a rejected valid complaint, which is reversible but can trigger escalation or regulatory complaints.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's billing rules, meter and tariff data and complaint policies, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The tester reads requirements and writes test cases, usually in a test management tool, so most time is writing; scripts are a minority.
length_reasoning: A small feature needs a short set of cases in under an hour; a complex feature with many paths and data variations takes most of a day.
review_reasoning: A test lead reads the cases against the requirements to check coverage and clarity.
stakes_reasoning: Missing cases let defects through to later testing or users, usually caught and fixed at moderate cost.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the product's behaviour and the team's test conventions, built over weeks.

domain_reasoning: A test plan is a document built from reading requirements and writing scope, approach and schedule.
length_reasoning: A plan for a small change is a short page in an hour or two; a release plan with risks, environments and resourcing takes a couple of days.
review_reasoning: A test lead reads the plan and checks scope and risks against the requirements.
stakes_reasoning: A weak plan leaves gaps in testing that show up later as escaped defects, costly but recoverable.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the product, its release process and the team's risk tolerance, built over weeks to months.

domain_reasoning: Most of the time goes into running tests by operating the application and test tools, not writing code.
length_reasoning: A small change is retested in an hour or two; a large change with regression runs and defect write-ups takes a few days.
review_reasoning: A release manager reads the results summary, checks defects and spot-checks some failed and passed cases.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong sign-off can send a defective change to production, causing outages or user impact.
context_reasoning: Needs the product's expected behaviour, environments and release criteria, built over months.

domain_reasoning: The worker types the summary and picks codes in the contact-centre or CRM system, mostly operating forms.
length_reasoning: A routine call takes a minute or two to wrap up; a complex call with several actions takes about five minutes.
review_reasoning: A QA reviewer opens the record and compares it with the call, but most records are only skimmed.
stakes_reasoning: A poor record causes confusion for the next agent or a missed follow-up, noticed and corrected cheaply.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's disposition codes and notes conventions, learned within a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: The worker opens the account or order system, checks the change and updates the case, which is operating systems.
length_reasoning: Confirming a simple change takes a few minutes; tracing a discrepancy across billing and order records takes longer.
review_reasoning: A supervisor opens the case and the account screen to confirm the change was made.
stakes_reasoning: A missed discrepancy leaves a wrong bill or service that the customer later complains about, reversible.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's systems and what a correct change looks like, learned over a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: Updating automated scripts means changing code and running it in the pipeline.
length_reasoning: A small locator or step change takes under an hour; a major product change that breaks many scripts takes a day or more.
review_reasoning: A code reviewer reads the diff and checks the pipeline run and that tests still verify the right behaviour.
stakes_reasoning: A script that passes but no longer checks the right thing hides defects, usually found later and fixed.
context_reasoning: Needs the test framework, codebase and product behaviour, built over weeks to a couple of months.

domain_reasoning: Most of the time goes into operating imaging tools, admin consoles and account systems, with some waiting while installs run.
length_reasoning: A standard image with routine software takes about an hour of active work; a role needing special software and access takes several hours.
review_reasoning: An IT supervisor checks a configured machine against a checklist, signing in and verifying software and accounts.
stakes_reasoning: A missed setting or access problem is noticed by the employee quickly and fixed, though missed security settings can matter.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's images, software list and account procedures, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The reviewer reads code and standards documents and writes recommendations, mostly reading and writing text and code without changing it.
length_reasoning: A small program is checked in under an hour; a large build with many deviations takes a day.
review_reasoning: A QA lead or developer checks the findings against the code and standard, which means opening many cited locations.
stakes_reasoning: A missed or wrong deviation causes rework or later compliance findings, usually fixed in development.
context_reasoning: Needs the applicable standards and the team's code base and conventions, built over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The tester reads logs, config files and code to find the failure source, which is working with code and configuration.
length_reasoning: A clear failure with an obvious log entry takes minutes; an intermittent one needs an hour or more of tracing.
review_reasoning: A developer reads the diagnosis and checks it against the log and code; trivial ones take a glance.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong diagnosis sends developers the wrong way and costs time, caught when the fix does not work.
context_reasoning: Needs deep knowledge of the system's architecture, logging and past defects, built over months.

domain_reasoning: The worker fills in vendor portals or forms and updates the ticket, which is operating websites and tools.
length_reasoning: A simple RMA with warranty data takes about ten minutes; a complex problem needing logs and diagnostics takes longer.
review_reasoning: An IT supervisor checks the case details, warranty info and ticket update.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong or incomplete referral delays repair and annoys the user, but is fixed by resubmitting.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's assets, warranty and vendor contracts, learned over a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: Most time goes into running the build on many configurations and recording results, operating test environments and tools.
length_reasoning: A small matrix takes a few hours; a large matrix of browsers, devices and systems takes days.
review_reasoning: A QA lead reads the results and filed issues and re-runs a few combinations to confirm.
stakes_reasoning: Missed incompatibilities reach users on specific platforms, causing support load and patches.
context_reasoning: Needs the product, supported platforms and test setup, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: Setting up a tracker project means configuring fields and workflows in a defect-tracking tool.
length_reasoning: A simple project from a template is a couple of hours; a custom workflow with permissions and integrations takes a few days.
review_reasoning: A QA manager walks through the fields and workflow in the tool and tries a test defect.
stakes_reasoning: Poor configuration causes inconvenience and rework of data, fixed by changing settings.
context_reasoning: Needs the team's process and tool setup, learned over weeks.

unit_flag_reason: Feasibility studies range from a quick cost comparison to a full workflow and space redesign, so the item mixes very different kinds of work.
domain_reasoning: The study is mostly gathering information, analysing and writing a report with a recommendation.
length_reasoning: A small cost comparison takes a day or so; a full study with workflow analysis and space design takes weeks of active work.
review_reasoning: An IT manager reads the report and checks key figures and assumptions.
stakes_reasoning: A flawed recommendation can lead to a costly investment decision that is hard to reverse.
context_reasoning: Needs deep knowledge of the organisation's workflows, systems and people, built over months.

domain_reasoning: The worker writes a how-to document, with screenshots, mostly writing text.
length_reasoning: A short how-to takes an hour; a full guide with screenshots and testing takes a day.
review_reasoning: A supervisor reads the guide and tries the steps to confirm they work.
stakes_reasoning: Wrong steps cause user confusion and extra tickets, fixed by editing the document.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's systems and user population, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The tester reproduces the problem in the product and reads logs, which is operating applications and tools.
length_reasoning: A reproducible issue takes under an hour; an elusive one needs several hours.
review_reasoning: A developer reads the findings and may try the reproduction steps.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong finding leaves the customer's problem unresolved or sends developers astray, but is reversed once noticed.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the product, its versions and customer configurations, built over months.
